market_context: United States; sweet potatoes, especially orange-fleshed varieties
title: Sweet potato: calories, fiber, carbohydrates and nutrients

seo.title: Sweet potato: calories, fiber, carbohydrates and nutrients
seo.meta_description: Raw sweet potato provides about 86 calories, 20.1 g carbohydrate, 3 g fiber and 1.6 g protein per 100 g. Orange-fleshed varieties are also exceptionally rich in beta-carotene, a vitamin A precursor.
seo.search_intent: Explain sweet-potato nutrition per 100 grams and how cooking, water content, flesh color and serving size change the numbers.

excerpt: A USDA reference for raw sweet potato provides about 86 calories, 20.1 g carbohydrate, 3 g fiber, 1.6 g protein and almost no fat per 100 g. Orange-fleshed varieties are notably rich in beta-carotene; boiling or baking changes per-100-gram values because the finished food contains a different amount of water.
content_html:
Sweet potatoes are sometimes described either as “too sugary” or as a nutritional superfood. The useful middle ground is simpler: they are a water-rich starchy vegetable with fiber, very little fat and micronutrients that vary substantially by flesh color.

What 100 grams provides

A USDA raw sweet-potato reference contains about 86 calories, 20.1 g carbohydrate, 3.0 g fiber, 1.57 g protein and 0.05 g fat per 100 g.

NutrientPer 100 g raw
Calories86 kcal
Carbohydrate20.1 g
Fiber3.0 g
Protein1.57 g
Fat0.05 g
Potassium337 mg

A 200 g amount would correspond to roughly 172 calories and 6 g fiber before accounting for cooking-related water changes.

Cooking changes concentration

A USDA reference for boiled sweet potato without skin provides about 76 calories, 17.7 g carbohydrate and 2.5 g fiber per 100 g. Its higher water content leaves nutrients slightly less concentrated by weight than the raw reference.

Baking can move the other direction because more water evaporates. That does not mean the oven creates calories; the finished food simply contains less water per 100 grams.

Why orange sweet potatoes stand out for vitamin A

Orange flesh is rich in beta-carotene, which the body can convert to vitamin A. NIH lists one baked sweet potato in its skin at about 1,403 micrograms RAE vitamin A, or 156% of the U.S. Daily Value used in that table.

That figure does not apply equally to white, yellow and purple varieties, which have different carotenoid and anthocyanin profiles.

Are sweet potatoes high in sugar?

The carbohydrate includes both starch and sugars. Cooking can make the potato taste sweeter as starch is broken down and transformed. But sweetness alone does not describe the food's fiber, water, potassium and carotenoid content.

Preparation still matters

Boiled, steamed or plainly baked sweet potato remains moderate in energy density. Deep frying or adding substantial oil, butter, sugar or sauces can push the dish much higher.

The useful nutritional identity

Sweet potato is mainly a carbohydrate food, not a major protein or fat source. For orange varieties, beta-carotene is the most distinctive micronutrient feature, while total calories depend on both serving size and preparation.

Preparation changes calories per bite more than the sweet potato itself

A plain baked or boiled sweet potato is mostly water and carbohydrate with very little fat. Frying or coating it generously with oil can raise calorie density substantially because the added fat contributes about nine calories per gram. Toppings matter in the same way: butter, sugar, marshmallows, cheese, or creamy sauces can transform a relatively simple starchy vegetable into a much richer dish.

Boiling may cause some water-soluble nutrients to move into the cooking water, while baking concentrates flavor as moisture is lost. Neither method makes the food categorically “good” or “bad.” The useful comparison is the finished portion and what has been added.

Orange, purple, and white varieties are nutritionally different

Orange-fleshed sweet potatoes are especially rich in beta-carotene, which the body can convert to vitamin A. Purple varieties contain anthocyanin pigments, while white or cream-colored varieties have a different carotenoid profile. All provide carbohydrate, potassium, and some fiber, but color can signal meaningful differences in plant compounds.

The skin contributes fiber and can be eaten when it is clean and in good condition. Leaving it on also reduces food waste. People who prefer a smoother texture can peel the potato without losing the entire nutritional value; most of the carbohydrate and many nutrients remain in the flesh.

Sweet potatoes can fit both high- and moderate-carbohydrate meals

Because they are starchy, sweet potatoes contribute more carbohydrate than non-starchy vegetables such as leafy greens, zucchini, or broccoli. Portion size therefore matters for people tracking carbohydrate intake. Pairing a sweet potato with protein, vegetables, and a source of fat creates a more complete meal than treating it as the only food on the plate.

Cooling cooked sweet potato can increase a small amount of resistant starch, although it does not turn the food into a low-carbohydrate item. For most people, the practical advantages are simpler: sweet potatoes are filling, versatile, naturally sweet, and nutrient-dense enough to serve as a regular starch alongside grains, potatoes, legumes, or other root vegetables.

Glycemic response also varies with cooking method, portion, and the rest of the meal. Mashing breaks the food structure more than eating intact chunks, while protein, fat, and fiber from other foods can slow the overall meal response. People managing blood glucose may find it more useful to test a realistic portion in a mixed meal than to treat every sweet potato preparation as metabolically identical.

faq.question: How many calories are in sweet potato?
faq.answer: Raw sweet potato is about 86 calories per 100 g; a USDA boiled, skinless reference is about 76 calories per 100 g.

faq.question: How much fiber is in sweet potato?
faq.answer: The raw USDA reference contains about 3 g fiber per 100 g, with variation by variety and preparation.

faq.question: Why is orange sweet potato high in vitamin A?
faq.answer: Its orange flesh is rich in beta-carotene, which the body can convert into vitamin A.
